clinicalPearls: A group of disorders caused by variants in genes encoding subunits of the NMDA-type glutamate receptor, with intellectual disability, hypotonia and often epilepsy
GRIN2A variants are characteristically linked to an epilepsy-aphasia spectrum, including speech disorders and epileptic encephalopathy with continuous spike-and-wave in sleep
GRIN1 and GRIN2B variants more often present with global developmental delay, movement disorders and autistic features
The functional effect spans a spectrum from loss-of-function to gain-of-function, which influences phenotype and potential targeted therapy
Movement disorders such as dystonia, chorea and stereotypies, plus cortical visual impairment, may accompany the picture
Caused predominantly by de novo autosomal dominant variants, though some loss-of-function GRIN2A families show inheritance
Understanding whether a variant enhances or reduces receptor activity can guide whether NMDA-modulating agents may help or harm
reference.pathophysiology: The genes GRIN1, GRIN2A and GRIN2B encode the GluN1, GluN2A and GluN2B subunits of the NMDA-type ionotropic glutamate receptor, a calcium-permeable channel central to excitatory neurotransmission and synaptic plasticity underlying learning and memory. Pathogenic variants alter receptor assembly, gating or ion permeation, producing either loss-of-function (reduced current) or gain-of-function (excessive or prolonged current) effects. This disturbed glutamatergic signalling disrupts activity-dependent circuit development, generating intellectual disability, epilepsy and movement abnormalities. Because both too little and too much receptor activity are harmful, the direction of the functional change is central to understanding and potentially treating each variant.
additionalDifferentials: Landau-Kleffner syndrome and epilepsy-aphasia spectrum of other causes
Other channelopathy-related developmental and epileptic encephalopathies
additionalInvestigations: EEG, including sleep recording to detect continuous spike-and-wave in slow-wave sleep
Brain MRI, often normal or with non-specific findings
Formal speech and language and neuropsychological assessment
Gene panel or exome sequencing covering GRIN1, GRIN2A and GRIN2B
Functional characterisation of the variant where available to determine gain- or loss-of-function
redFlags: Loss or regression of language skills
Cortical visual impairment or severe movement disorder impairing function
reference.prognosis: Outcome ranges from milder speech and learning difficulties to severe intellectual disability with drug-resistant epilepsy, depending on the gene and functional effect of the variant. Language and seizure burden are major determinants of function, and care is individualised and supportive.
pitfalls: Assuming all GRIN variants behave alike when loss- and gain-of-function require different approaches
Overlooking electrical status epilepticus in sleep by not recording sleep EEG
Using NMDA-modulating agents without knowing the variant's functional direction
Attributing the language disorder to hearing or environmental factors alone
management: Apply mechanism-directed therapy guided by the functional variant class, with NMDA-receptor antagonists such as memantine or dextromethorphan for gain-of-function variants and serine or co-agonist supplementation for loss-of-function variants
Treat epilepsy with antiseizure medication, including corticosteroid or benzodiazepine courses for continuous spike-and-wave in sleep seen in the GRIN2A epilepsy-aphasia phenotype
Manage movement disorders such as dystonia, chorea and stereotypies and provide symptomatic care for hypotonia and cortical visual impairment
Provide early developmental intervention with physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech, language and communication support
Coordinate multidisciplinary neurodevelopmental follow-up with periodic EEG and neuropsychological assessment
Offer genetic counselling for predominantly de novo autosomal dominant variants, with family testing where inherited loss-of-function is identified
